planting.note: Scatter seed directly onto disturbed, clay or rocky soil in autumn so winter rains trigger germination; skip supplemental water once seedlings establish.

directions: A classic California wildflower-mix annual, this phacelia is very easy, reseeds reliably, and produces a long spring-to-summer bloom of lavender-blue coiled flower clusters that draw native bees in large numbers. It thrives on neglect in lean sites where richer soil would favor weeds instead. Leave spent plants standing until seed shatters to let the stand perpetuate itself year to year.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall into sandy or rocky fast-draining soil in full sun; a light dusting of wood ash over seed improves germination, mimicking its post-fire chaparral ecology.

directions: The showiest-flowered annual phacelia, blooming up to an inch and a half wide, this species carries an upright columnar habit and exceptionally long winter-into-summer bloom window. Because it is adapted to colonize freshly burned chaparral, it performs best in newly disturbed or recently cleared ground rather than long-established beds. It needs almost no irrigation once up, making it one of the better backbone annuals for a dry wildflower meadow.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall into well-drained, adaptable soil along a coastal-influenced bank or rock garden where decumbent stems can sprawl over edges; never irrigate once established.

directions: One of the few perennial Phacelia species suited to gardens, this mounding coastal-bluff native carries pale blue-to-white flower coils from spring through summer and serves as a larval and nectar host supporting the endangered Mission blue butterfly in its native San Francisco Bay range. Unlike the annual phacelias, it persists for multiple seasons, so give it a permanent spot rather than treating it as a wildflower-mix filler. Light grooming after the long spring-summer bloom keeps the mound tidy without harming next year's growth.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall at a lightly shaded woodland edge or understory position matching dry Yellow Pine or Red Fir forest habitat.

directions: A tall part-shade perennial with unusual unfurling flower stalks that open greenish-white blooms sequentially over an extended period, this phacelia is documented to attract an exceptional range of native bee species. Use it where other Phacelia would scorch — a lightly shaded woodland edge matches its native forest habitat. Its name reflects strongly variable foliage shapes even on a single plant, giving it textural interest outside bloom time.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall into sandy or sandstone-derived, fast-draining soil in part shade; use locally sourced seed where possible given high regional variability.

directions: An unusually cold-hardy, spreading part-shade perennial surviving to -10 degrees Fahrenheit, this species has a long western range from British Columbia to the southwestern US, making it a tough, low-water groundcover-type phacelia distinct from the typical desert and chaparral annuals. It can be used well outside the mild-winter zones where most of its relatives are confined. Give it room to spread rather than crowding it among compact annuals.

planting.note: Direct-sow into sandy, gravelly wash-type soil in a desert garden setting; avoid any summer water, since it is strictly a cool-season desert ephemeral.

directions: A true hot-desert annual from the Mojave and Sonoran deserts, this phacelia carries deeply crenate, lobed foliage and violet-blue flowers blooming earlier, in winter and spring, than most California annual phacelias, extending the pollinator-forage calendar. It is adapted to the harshest, fastest-draining substrates and will rot in richer garden soil. It bridges the late-winter nectar gap for emerging native bees.

planting.note: Lightly dust sown seed with ash or charate before fall sowing into sandy or granular soil, mimicking its post-fire ecology; germinates poorly from untreated seed.

directions: A compact desert-gold-companion annual with distinctive blue-lavender flowers and a contrasting yellow throat, this phacelia is a reliable component of Mojave and San Joaquin Valley superbloom displays. It is a true desert ephemeral suited to rock gardens or desert wildflower plantings rather than conventional borders, and needs no water beyond natural winter precipitation. The yellow-throated blue flowers are a recognizable component of spring superbloom displays.
